summary: Four of the six prior findings are genuinely closed, measured rather than taken on report. Z2: the verbatim duplications are GONE -- a repeated-substring scan over M4.19 and M4.20 (every word 4-gram, and every clause split on -- / ; / , / warning marks) finds no repeat at all; the severed withZone sentence is now complete. Z1: the row names all three test classes with a seam for each, and the two split points (548, 524) now match the two class javadocs. Z5: the FaultFixtures extraction preserved every kill I re-ran -- 13 mutants, all killed: ambiguous putIfAbsent landing zeroes and landing via unconditional put; clean putIfAbsent landing zeroes; clean putIfMatch dropping the version; clean stat/get/list returning empty; List.copyOf -> unmodifiableList; Map.copyOf -> the live map; the duplicate second write deleted; the ambiguous putIfMatch landing write deleted. FaultFixtures needs no test of its own: mutating body() to a same-length zeroed array and read() to a constant empty string are BOTH killed by the three classes, so it is constrained by construction. Z3's row text is accurate -- AmbiguousPutStore.java:39-45 does carry Mode.LOST ('The store never saw it; the version is unchanged'), and both ambiguous arms (:209-222, :279-285) do attempt the write before throwing. Nothing here changes an object-store request rate: the decorator is test-only and its extra requests scale with faulted calls, not with records, shards, partitions or indices; M4.16's new row correctly rejects 'seal every unsealed ancestor' as unbounded failover work and prices the lease-check option per BATCH. What is wrong is the Z6 fix itself. The comment added to state the meter's position states it BACKWARDS in this project's own decorator vocabulary -- docs/research/30-design-space/07-pluggable-store-abstraction.md:151-154 calls CountingBinStore(GoverningBinStore(...)) 'Counting outside governing', so 'THE METER GOES OUTSIDE THIS DECORATOR, never inside' names exactly the composition that hides the injector's requests, while the snippet in the same sentence names the other one. And it is absolute where the right order depends on the question. Three minors follow, all recorded rather than blocking: the row's commit inventory omits FaultFixtures.java (third consecutive round that sentence is wrong), the class's reproducibility claim silently requires single-threaded driving, and M4.16 cites simulation evidence without the disclosure its two neighbouring rows carry. Also observed and NOT raised as findings, because neither has a failure scenario that survives scrutiny: the extraction left unused imports in all three classes (Body and ByteArrayInputStream in each, StandardCharsets in the two that use the fully-qualified name anyway, and a static import of FaultFixtures.read in FaultInjectingStoreStreamsTest which never calls it, which also makes FaultFixtures' javadoc 'the two fixtures the three test classes share' true of body but not of read); and four double-blank runs remain of the six raised as Z4 (FaultInjectingStoreTest:42,297 and FaultInjectingStoreStreamsTest:41,261). Z4's structural half is also unfixed -- theInjectedRecordIsASNAPSHOTACallerCannotMutate still sits in FaultInjectingStoreTest:252 while its other half sits in FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest:136 with a comment pointing across, and the class still holds one Faults(1.0,0,0) test under a javadoc whose seam is 'the CLEAN paths'. That was a minor last round and stays one: under review.md rule 11 it lands, and I am not re-raising it to justify a round.

findings.title: The comment added to fix Z6 states the meter's position INVERTED in this project's own decorator vocabulary, and states it as absolute when the correct order depends on which question the meter is answering.
findings.detail: The comment reads: '⚠️ THE METER GOES OUTSIDE THIS DECORATOR, never inside: wrap as `new FaultInjectingStore(new CountingBinStore(...), ...)` so the counter sees the requests this class ADDS -- the duplicate retry and the ambiguous landing write. Inverted, every injected request is invisible to the meter...'. In `new FaultInjectingStore(new CountingBinStore(...))` the meter is the DELEGATE -- inside the injector, below it in the chain. This repository fixes that vocabulary in writing: docs/research/30-design-space/07-pluggable-store-abstraction.md:151-154 shows `CountingBinStore( GoverningBinStore( ... ) )` and calls it 'Counting OUTSIDE governing', i.e. outside means the enclosing wrapper. So the capitalised imperative -- 'OUTSIDE ... never inside' -- names precisely the composition the rest of the sentence forbids, and the snippet, the rationale and the 'Inverted, ...' clause all name the other one. The one test that depends on the order, aDUPLICATEDPutREALLYREACHESTheStoreTwice... at FaultInjectingStoreTest.java:200-209, composes it the snippet's way and measures 2 puts. Second, separable problem: 'never inside' is absolute, and the order is not. Metering BELOW the injector counts what actually hit the store, including the harness's synthetic duplicate and the ambiguous landing write -- right for that test. Metering ABOVE it counts what the PRODUCTION caller asked for, which is what M4.9's bounded-recovery budget is about; below the injector, an injected duplicate inflates that budget for a reason the protocol is not responsible for. The comment gives one order for both questions and names neither question.
findings.failure_scenario: This comment exists only to be read by the next hand, and it is the whole content of the Z6 fix. M4.13's row commits to running the sweep, and M4.9's row commits to asserting bounded recovery 'by REQUEST COUNT through CountingBinStore'. A hand composing that harness reads the capitalised rule, writes `new CountingBinStore(new FaultInjectingStore(store, seed, faults))` -- also the natural reading of 'meter outermost, so it counts what the caller asked for' -- and every injected duplicate PUT and every ambiguous landing write becomes invisible to the meter. A recovery under faults then issues more conditional writes than it is budgeted for and reports the budget green: a cost threshold passing while the requests happen, which is the exact blindness cost.md R9 and CountingBinStore exist to close, and which no gate can see. The inverse mistake is live too: someone who obeys the snippet while asserting a PRODUCTION request budget under faults gets a bound inflated by harness duplicates and either relaxes the threshold (non-negotiable 2) or blames the protocol. Before this round the tree was silent on the order and a reader had to think; now it carries an authoritative-looking rule that is wrong as stated.
findings.suggestion: Say it in terms of the chain rather than in terms of 'outside', and say which question each order answers. Something like: 'the meter is the DELEGATE of this decorator (`new FaultInjectingStore(new CountingBinStore(...), ...)`) when the assertion is about what reached the store -- the duplicate retry and the ambiguous landing write are real requests; put the meter ABOVE it only when the assertion is about what the production caller issued, as M4.9's recovery budget is, and say so at the call site.' Resolution is one sentence, not a split: rule 12's split remedy is aimed at majors arriving from new surface, and this one is a single comment introduced this round. A staged baselines/review.txt entry arguing the snippet disambiguates the headline is the other legitimate exit.

findings.title: The row's WHAT THIS COMMIT CONTAINS sentence is wrong again, for the third consecutive round: five new Java files are staged and it accounts for four. FaultFixtures.java appears nowhere in backlog.md.
findings.detail: The sentence now reads 'the decorator plus THREE test classes: `FaultInjectingStoreTest` ... `FaultInjectingStoreStreamsTest` ... and `FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest`', which is exactly right about those four files. The staged set is FIVE new files: those four plus sequencer/src/test/java/binjava/sequencer/FaultFixtures.java, the 42-line shared fixture holder created this round. `grep -c FaultFixtures docs/internal/product/backlog.md` returns 0, and the row contains neither the word 'fixture' nor any mention of the de-duplication. The mechanism is identical to the two previous failures of this same sentence: a review round's fix added a file, and the enumeration was not extended. The row already knows the general shape of this problem -- '⚠️ NO COUNT HERE, deliberately: this sentence said "six", then "nine", then "twelve", and was wrong at every one -- a number in prose is stale the moment a review round adds a test' -- and then commits the same error one abstraction up, with names instead of numbers.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.15 is M4's milestone review, and milestone-review/SKILL.md reads backlog.md, which AGENTS.md calls authoritative. A reader reconciling this row against the tree finds a fifth file the row does not account for and has to decide whether it is silent scope widening (AGENTS.md 'Never widen scope silently') or a stray from the M4.19/M4.20 split like the five untracked files. Weaker than the Z1 instance and that is why this is minor: deleting FaultFixtures.java breaks compilation of all three test classes, so unlike FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest it cannot be dropped with the suite still green. The residual cost is a reader's minute and a row that has now mis-described its own commit three rounds running.
findings.suggestion: Either add the clause -- 'plus `FaultFixtures`, the shared `body`/`read` holder that stopped the fixture being copied three times across classes that exist to be compared against each other' -- or stop enumerating files in prose and let the commit's own file list be the inventory. The second is the row's own argument about counts, applied to names; if the enumeration is worth having it is worth deriving (gate-design rung 2), because this is the third round an agent has been asked to keep a file list in sync by hand and the third time it has not.

findings.title: The class's central claim -- a seed replays a run exactly -- silently requires single-threaded driving, and nothing says so, while the next consumer's stated criteria are 'many logical pods'.
findings.detail: `injected` is a bare ArrayList (:95) and `drawCounts` a bare TreeMap (:96), mutated on every faulting call and on every draw; the three `Random`s are drawn in a fixed order per call. The javadoc promises '⚠️ SEEDED AND REPLAYABLE. The whole value of a simulation is that a failing seed is a permanent, named regression rather than a story about a flake', and theSameSeedInjectsTheSameFaultsSoAFailingRunIsAPermanentRegression (FaultInjectingStoreStreamsTest.java:262) pins it -- single-threaded. Under two threads the promise fails three separate ways: interleaved draws make the fault sequence depend on scheduling, `drawCounts.merge` on a TreeMap is a data race, and `List.copyOf(injected)` over a concurrently-appended ArrayList can throw or copy a torn state. Nothing in the class states the precondition, no test would notice, and the surrounding package is not obviously single-threaded -- LeaseManagerConcurrencyTest.java exists, and AGENTS.md names virtual threads as this project's default concurrency construct.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.20's row states its acceptance criteria as 'many logical pods, one seed, driven through the `Sequencer` seam'. The obvious implementation of 'many pods' in this codebase is one virtual thread per pod sharing one store. The moment that happens the seed stops reproducing the run: M4.13's sweep reports a violating seed, the next hand re-runs that seed, and it passes -- so the defect is filed as a flake and the sweep's whole value proposition, which this class's javadoc calls 'the whole value of a simulation', quietly evaporates. The ConcurrentModificationException is the lucky outcome; the unlucky one is a silently different fault sequence per run.
findings.suggestion: One javadoc line: 'NOT thread-safe, and deliberately -- reproducibility requires the pods be driven one call at a time from a single thread; concurrency belongs in the driver's interleaving, not in the store.' That also tells M4.20 how to build 'many logical pods' (interleave logically on one thread) instead of discovering it after a flake.

findings.title: The new M4.16 row rests its central claim on evidence from a simulation that is not in the tree, and omits the untracked disclosure that both of its neighbouring new rows carry.
findings.detail: M4.16 is added by this diff and says '⚠️ FOUND BY THE SIMULATION, which is what it was built for', then reports measured detail from it -- seed 14's dump, '39 epochs burned for 8 commits', '73 epochs for 3 takeovers', seeds 45 and 79, 'SEED 79 VIOLATED WITH ZERO SUCCESSFUL ZOMBIE WRITES'. The simulation is CommitProtocolSimulation.java, which is untracked and deferred to M4.20; a fresh clone has none of it. The same diff's M4.19 and M4.20 rows each disclose exactly this about themselves ('⚠️ NEITHER IS TRACKED YET, so this row delivers the CLASS as well as its fixtures and a fresh clone has none of it', and '⚠️ NEITHER `CommitProtocolSimulation` NOR `SimulatedClock` IS TRACKED YET'), so the standard was set inside this commit and M4.16 is the row that does not meet it. The row's mechanism claim is independently checkable and I checked it -- LocalSequencer.java:83 does compute `long prevEpoch = epoch - 1` and :94 seals only that one -- so the defect is real; it is the provenance of the numbers that is unsupported by the tree.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.16 is FR-11/NFR-11 and its deliverable is ADR-0029, a decision between four candidates weighed partly on these measurements. A hand picking it up in a fresh clone reads 'FOUND BY THE SIMULATION', looks for the simulation, and finds nothing -- and cannot tell whether it was deleted, never written, or lives somewhere else. The most likely outcomes are the two the neighbouring rows were edited to prevent: the numbers are re-derived from scratch at the cost of the session, or they are carried into the ADR as fact because a backlog row asserted them, which is the same defect as this row's own '"IS DRAFTED", which was true only of a scratch file OUTSIDE the repository -- nothing in the tree may rest on a draft the tree cannot see.'
findings.suggestion: One clause: 'the simulation that found it is M4.20's `CommitProtocolSimulation`, NOT YET TRACKED, so these numbers came from a working copy and must be re-measured once it lands.' Same sentence the two adjacent rows already carry.
